title: Man standing when struck from behind, witness says
article: Jeffrey Michael Berg was standing still, his hands spread on the trunk of a car in an east side Vancouver alley, when a Vancouver police officer struck him from behind with his gun, then kicked him twice in the back of the neck as he lay on the ground, a witness told a coroner's inquest Friday.
Berg died two days later in hospital from a heart attack caused by an aneurysm. An autopsy found the aneurysm was the result of a blow to the side of his neck.

Berg and three other men were in a car that was rammed by a police cruiser driven by Const. David Bruce-Thomas, shortly after Berg and another man burst into a nearby house where they mistakenly thought there was a marijuana growing operation. They were fleeing when Bruce-Thomas stopped them.

Sari Fujikawa told the coroner's inquest jury of four men and one woman that she was visiting her parents at their home on Oct. 22, 2000, when she heard a noise in the alley and went outside to see what was happening.

She said she saw a red car stopped against a garage, and a man later identified as Berg standing at the back of it with his hands on the trunk and his legs slightly apart. She said a police officer was approaching him, holding his gun out in a two-handed grip and yelling something she couldn't make out.
Reading from a statement she wrote three months after the events of that night, Fujikawa was briefly overcome with emotion, dabbing her eyes with a tissue before she continued.

"The officer was still yelling and he walked toward the man until he was standing behind him," she said. "The officer knocked the man down with his gun in his right hand. The officer kicked the man in the back of the head brutally two times with his right foot.
"I felt sick, angry, numbed and shocked at the same time. The man had not moved toward the officer in any threatening way. From what I could see, he was standing still like a statue."

Fujikawa said Berg was unconscious in a fetal position on the ground, and the officer grabbed him by his clothing and pulled him, face-down, across the alley. She said she clearly remembered how Berg's feet dragged --"like a doll's."

The jury watched several minutes of silent video footage shot by a nearby resident, starting with several officers standing in the vicinity of Berg's still form. The camera stops, and starts again to show paramedics working for several minutes on Berg, pumping his chest before taking him away on a stretcher -- the last sequence on the videotape.

Under cross-examination by Bill Smart, the lawyer for Bruce- Thomas, Fujikawa admitted she could not see the exact point of impact as the police officer brought his gun down on Berg because Bruce-Thomas's head obscured that part of her view. However, she said the blow landed somewhere around the neck or upper part of Berg's body.

The third day of the coroner's inquest was marked by wrangling between lawyer Cameron Ward, who is representing Berg's family, and coroner's counsel John Bethell, as well as three other lawyers representing the police department, the officer who struck Berg, and the City of Vancouver.

At one point, after Ward objected to Bethell's line of questioning, Bethell warned coroner Jeannine Robinson: "If my friend keeps making allegations of bias, there are going to be serious consequences for this inquest."

Ward responded that Bethell was asking Fujikawa questions that anticipated the police version of events, calling it "completely improper," and adding that Bethell's role "is to ask the witness what she saw with non-leading questions."

At that point, Bethell offered to quit as coroner's counsel, but his offer was turned down by the coroner, who said: "I don't want this to turn into a catfight, at it seems to be turning into at every step of the way."

Outside the courtroom, Ward played down the exchange. "From my perspective, it's not unusual when you have several lawyers representing the police interests and then myself only representing a different interest."
